solution:
**(B)** liberate oxygen

Oxygen is released only in the light reaction, when water is split by photosystem II in the thylakoids of the chloroplast. A cell without chloroplasts cannot photosynthesise, so it cannot liberate oxygen. It still respires, so it evolves carbon dioxide, needs water and uses carbohydrates as food.

**(C)** ATP

The light reaction traps solar energy as ATP (with \(\text{NADPH}_2\) as reducing power), and these two molecules carry that energy into the stroma, where the dark reaction uses them to reduce \(\text{CO}_2\). Chlorophyll traps light but stays in the thylakoid, ADP is the spent form returned to the light reaction, and RuBP is the \(\text{CO}_2\) acceptor of the Calvin cycle, not an energy carrier.

**(C)** It is characteristic of \(\text{C}_4\)-plants

The question asks for the WRONG statement. Photorespiration is a wasteful process linked with the \(\text{C}_3\) cycle; in \(\text{C}_4\) plants the high \(\text{CO}_2\) concentration in the bundle sheath keeps Rubisco acting as a carboxylase, so there is no photorespiration. It does begin in the chloroplast (where Rubisco oxygenates RuBP) and it needs light, so it happens only in the day time.

**(D)** both 'b' and 'c'

Non-cyclic photophosphorylation uses both PS I and PS II. Because PS II splits water to replace its lost electrons, oxygen is evolved, and because the electrons end up reducing \(\text{NADP}^+\), it forms both ATP and \(\text{NADPH}_2\), the assimilatory power. Cyclic photophosphorylation involves only PS I, makes ATP alone and evolves no oxygen, so using only PS I describes the cyclic process, not the non-cyclic one.

**(B)** 18 ATP and 12 \(\text{NADPH}_2\)

Six turns of the Calvin cycle fix 6 \(\text{CO}_2\) and make one glucose. Each turn uses 3 ATP and 2 \(\text{NADPH}_2\) (12 ATP and 12 \(\text{NADPH}_2\) to reduce 12 molecules of 3-PGA, plus 6 ATP to regenerate 6 RuBP), giving 18 ATP and 12 \(\text{NADPH}_2\). The figure of 30 ATP is the cost of the \(\text{C}_4\) pathway, not of the Calvin cycle.

As printed, no option is correct: the phrase "in bundle sheath cells" contradicts the intended answer.

Maize is a \(\text{C}_4\) plant and wheat a \(\text{C}_3\) plant, so their first stable products of \(\text{CO}_2\) fixation are OAA (oxaloacetic acid) and 3PGA respectively, which is the pairing "OAA and 3PGA" the question means. But in maize the OAA is formed in the mesophyll cells by PEP carboxylase; the bundle sheath cells of maize run the Calvin cycle, where the first stable product is 3PGA. "OAA and PEPA" and "OAA and OAA" are wrong for wheat, and "3PGA and OAA" reverses the two plants. Read without the words "in bundle sheath cells", the answer is OAA and 3PGA.

**(C)** prophyrin and phyrol respictively

This option is "porphyrin and phytol respectively" with misprints. A chlorophyll molecule has a head of tetrapyrrole, the porphyrin ring, and a long hydrocarbon tail called phytol attached to it. Phytin is a different compound (a phosphate store in seeds), not the tail of chlorophyll, and the head is the whole tetrapyrrole ring, not a single pyrrole, nor is the tail a pyrrole.

**(C)** proton, electron and oxygen

When electron-deficient PS II oxidises water, protons, electrons and oxygen are all released: \(4\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{O}_2 + 4\text{H}^+ + 4e^-\). The electrons refill PS II, the protons go to reduce \(\text{NADP}^+\) and build the proton gradient, and the oxygen is given out. Each of the other options leaves out one of these three products.

**(B)** 3ATP + 2\(\text{NADPH}_2\)

Fixing 6 \(\text{CO}_2\) into one glucose needs 18 ATP and 12 \(\text{NADPH}_2\), so one \(\text{CO}_2\) needs one sixth of that: 3 ATP and 2 \(\text{NADPH}_2\). Two ATP and two \(\text{NADPH}_2\) reduce the two 3-PGA molecules formed per \(\text{CO}_2\), and the third ATP regenerates RuBP.

**(D)** PGA and phosphoglycolate

At high oxygen concentration Rubisco acts as an oxygenase: RuBP reacts with \(\text{O}_2\) instead of \(\text{CO}_2\) and forms one 3-carbon PGA and one 2-carbon phosphoglycolate. This starts photorespiration. Malic acid and PEP belong to the \(\text{C}_4\) pathway and are not products of Rubisco.

**(C)** PQ, Cytochrome, PC and FeS

Electrons leaving PS II pass to plastoquinone (PQ), then through the cytochrome \(b_6f\) complex to plastocyanin (PC), which hands them to PS I. From PS I they go on to the iron-sulphur (FeS) centres and ferredoxin on the way to \(\text{NADP}^+\), so FeS comes after PC, never first. Every other order breaks the PQ, cytochrome, PC sequence.

[Note: the chapter does not state this; standard biology gives the Z-scheme order PS II, PQ, cytochrome \(b_6f\), PC, PS I, FeS, ferredoxin.]
